Lesson A0-02: Introducing Yourself ​

Level: A0 (Foundations)
CEFR Level: A0
Duration: 75 minutes
New Vocabulary: 32 words
Grammar Focus: Present tense of "zijn" (to be) and "hebben" (to have); personal pronouns in context; yes/no questions; possessive pronouns; negation with "niet"

Lesson Goal ​

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to introduce yourself (name, age, nationality, origin, languages spoken, family) and ask others these same questions in both informal and formal Dutch.

Previous Knowledge ​

You must have completed A0-01: Understanding Sounds before starting this lesson.

From A0-01, you should know:

  • Dutch alphabet and letter sounds
  • Dutch vowel sounds and diphthongs (aa, ee, oo, uu, ei, ou, etc.)
  • Stress patterns and basic pronunciation rules
  • How to recognize and repeat Dutch words

This lesson builds on your ability to recognize sounds and introduces your first complete sentences using grammar and meaningful vocabulary.

Why This Matters ​

Introductions are the foundation of every real conversation. You need to tell people who you are, where you come from, what languages you speak, and ask them the same questions back. This lesson teaches you the grammar and vocabulary to have a genuine first interaction in Dutch. These are skills you'll use repeatedly, in person and online, whenever you meet someone new.

Grammar ​

This lesson introduces five core grammar concepts needed for self-introduction:

1. Present Tense of "Zijn" (To Be) ​

The verb "zijn" is irregular and essential. Here is the conjugation:

PronounFormExample
ikbenIk ben Anna. (I am Anna.)
jij/jebentJij bent achttien. (You are eighteen.)
ubentU bent meneer Jansen. (You are Mr. Jansen.)
hij/zij/hetisHij is Nederlands. (He is Dutch.)
wij/wezijnWij zijn Turks. (We are Turkish.)
julliezijnJullie zijn kinderen. (You all are children.)
zij/zezijnZij zijn ouders. (They are parents.)

Key Pattern: The form changes with each pronoun. You must memorize these forms.

2. Present Tense of "Hebben" (To Have) ​

The verb "hebben" is also irregular. Here is the conjugation:

PronounFormExample
ikhebIk heb een broer. (I have a brother.)
jij/jehebtJij hebt een zus. (You have a sister.)
uhebt / heeftU hebt/heeft een familie. (You have a family.)
hij/zij/hetheeftHij heeft een moeder. (He has a mother.)
wij/wehebbenWij hebben een vader. (We have a father.)
julliehebbenJullie hebben kinderen. (You all have children.)
zij/zehebbenZij hebben familie. (They have family.)

Key Pattern: Like "zijn," the form changes with each pronoun. You must memorize these forms.

3. Personal Pronouns in Context ​

Personal pronouns you learned in A0-01 now appear in sentences. Review:

DutchEnglishUsage
ikIWhen talking about yourself
jij/jeyou (informal)When talking to one person casually
uyou (formal)When talking to someone formally; people you don't know well
hijheWhen talking about a man or masculine noun
zijshe / theyWhen talking about a woman (she) or multiple people (they)
wij/weweWhen talking about a group including yourself

Note: "je" is the unstressed form of "jij"; "we" is the unstressed form of "wij." They mean the same thing.

4. Yes/No Questions (Word Order Inversion) ​

To ask a yes/no question in Dutch, put the conjugated verb first, then the subject, then the rest:

Pattern: Verb + Subject + Rest

StatementQuestionEnglish
Jij bent Emma.Ben jij Emma?Are you Emma?
U bent meneer Jansen.Bent u meneer Jansen?Are you Mr. Jansen?
Hij is Nederlands.Is hij Nederlands?Is he Dutch?
Jij heb een broer.Heb je een broer?Do you have a brother?
Jullie zijn familie.Zijn jullie familie?Are you all family?

Important: Dutch does not use "do" or "does" in questions. Simply invert the verb and subject.

5. Possessive Pronouns and "Niet" (Negation) ​

Possessive Pronouns:

DutchEnglishExample
mijnmyMijn naam is Anna. (My name is Anna.)
jouw / jeyour (informal)Jouw naam / Je naam is...? (Your name is...?)
uwyour (formal)Uw naam is...? (Your name is...? formal)
zijnhisZijn vader is Turks. (His father is Turkish.)
haarherHaar moeder is Pools. (Her mother is Polish.)
ons / onzeourOns huis / Onze kinderen... (Our house / Our children...)
jullieyour (plural)Jullie familie is groot. (Your family is big.)
huntheirHun kinderen zijn hier. (Their children are here.)

Negation with "Niet":

The word "niet" means "not." Place it after the main verb or adjective:

DutchEnglish
Ik ben niet Duits.I am not German.
Zij is niet Spaans.She is not Spanish.
Wij zijn niet uit Frankrijk.We are not from France.
Ik kom niet uit Amerika.I am not from America.
Zij hebben niet een broer. (Formal)They do not have a brother.

Note: In everyday Dutch, "Ik heb geen broer" is more common than "Ik ben niet een broer," but both structures work at A0.

Grammar Reasoning ​

Why "Zijn" and "Hebben" Matter ​

"Zijn" (to be) and "hebben" (to have) are the two most common verbs in Dutch. You'll use them constantly:

  • Zijn: For identity, nationality, origin, age, emotion, location

    • Ik ben Anna. (I am Anna.)
    • Ik ben Turks. (I am Turkish.)
    • Ik ben twintig. (I am twenty.)

  • Hebben: For possession, family, and quantity

    • Ik heb een broer. (I have a brother.)
    • Ik heb een zus. (I have a sister.)

Why "Zijn" and "Hebben" Are Irregular ​

English speakers expect verbs to follow a pattern (I have, you have, he has, etc.). Dutch's "zijn" and "hebben" don't follow a predictable pattern--they're irregular because they're ancient words that have been used for thousands of years. Many irregular verbs in European languages are the most common verbs because they're so old.

You can't predict them; you must memorize them. This is normal and expected for language learners.

Why Word Order Changes in Questions ​

In English, we say "Are you Emma?" and "Do you have a brother?" In Dutch, the structure is the same: verb + subject. But Dutch is stricter about this rule than English is. You must invert for every question:

  • Ben jij Emma? (Are you Emma?)
  • Heb je een broer? (Do you have a brother?)
  • Kom je uit Nederland? (Do you come from the Netherlands?)

This is a pattern that will apply to almost every verb in Dutch, so learning it now saves time later.

Why "Niet" Comes After the Verb ​

English speakers often want to put "not" at the beginning ("Not I am...") or between the subject and verb ("I not am..."). Dutch requires "niet" to come after the main verb or complement:

  • Ik ben niet Duits. (I am not German.)
  • Ik kom niet uit Nederland. (I am not from the Netherlands.)

This position is consistent across tenses and sentence structures, so learning it now prevents confusion later.

Why "Jij" vs "U" ​

Dutch distinguishes formal and informal address. This is common in European languages (German has "du" vs "Sie," Spanish has "tú" vs "usted"). English doesn't have this distinction anymore, but it used to ("thou" vs "you").

  • Jij: Friends, family, classmates, young people, casual situations
  • U: Strangers, people older than you, people in positions of authority, formal situations

When in doubt, use "u." Dutch people will tell you to switch to "jij" if appropriate.

Pronunciation ​

Dutch pronunciation is generally consistent once you know the sound patterns from A0-01.

Key Sounds for This Lesson ​

Pronoun Sounds:

  • ik (ikh) -- Like the "k" in English "back"
  • jij (yay) -- Like the letter "J" in English (soft y sound)
  • u (oo) -- Like the "oo" in English "food"
  • hij (hay) -- Like the "ai" in "wait" (long i sound)
  • zij (zay) -- Like "z" + "ay" (voiced s + long i)
  • wij (way) -- Like the "ai" in "wait"
  • we (wuh) -- Like "w" + the "e" in "bet"

Verb Sounds:

  • ben (ben) -- Like English "bet" (short e sound)
  • bent (bent) -- Like English "bent" (short e, ending in t)
  • is (iss) -- Like English "is"
  • zijn (zine) -- Like "z" + the long i sound in "ice"
  • heb (hep) -- Like "h" + the "e" in "bet"
  • hebt (hept) -- Like "h" + the "e" in "bet" + "t"
  • heeft (hayft) -- Like "h" + the "ai" in "wait" + "ft"
  • hebben (HAH-buh) -- Stress the first syllable; sounds like "HAH-ben"

Country and Nationality Sounds:

  • Nederland (NAY-der-lahnt) -- Stress the first syllable, rhymes with "day"
  • Nederlands (NAY-der-lahnts) -- Same stress
  • Frankrijk (FRAHNK-ryk) -- Stress the first syllable
  • Spanje (SPAHN-yuh) -- Stress the first syllable, rhymes with "spa"
  • Polen (POH-len) -- Stress the first syllable
  • Turkije (tur-KEE-yuh) -- Stress the middle syllable
  • Roemenië (roo-MAY-nee-uh) -- Stress the middle syllable

Stress and Rhythm ​

Dutch stress the first syllable of most nouns and adjectives. When you see a capital letter, emphasize that syllable:

  • NAHM (name)
  • MOO-der (mother)
  • VAH-der (father)
  • BROOR (brother)
  • ZUS (sister)

If a word is longer, only the first syllable gets the main stress:

  • FAH-mee-lee (family)
  • NED-er-LAHND (Netherlands) -- Actually, both syllables get some stress

Listen to native speakers online to hear the natural rhythm.

Dialogue ​

Here are four realistic dialogues showing how to introduce yourself in different contexts.

Dialogue 1: Informal Greeting ​

Dutch:

A: Hoi. Ik ben Anna.
B: Hoi Anna. Ik ben Daan.
A: Aangenaam.
B: Aangenaam.

Translation:

A: Hi. I am Anna.
B: Hi Anna. I am Daan.
A: Nice to meet you.
B: Nice to meet you.

Dialogue 2: Asking Name and Age (Informal) ​

Dutch:

A: Hoe heet jij?
B: Mijn naam is Emma. Hoe heet jij?
A: Ik ben Lars. Ben jij twintig?
B: Nee, ik ben achttien.

Translation:

A: What is your name?
B: My name is Emma. What is your name?
A: I am Lars. Are you twenty?
B: No, I am eighteen.

Dialogue 3: Formal Introduction (Nationality and Language) ​

Dutch:

A: Goedemorgen. Hoe heet u?
B: Mijn naam is Sophie.
A: Waar komt u vandaan?
B: Ik kom uit België. Ik ben Belgisch.
A: Spreekt u Engels?
B: Ja, ik spreek Engels en Nederlands.

Translation:

A: Good morning. What is your name?
B: My name is Sophie.
A: Where are you from?
B: I am from Belgium. I am Belgian.
A: Do you speak English?
B: Yes, I speak English and Dutch.

Dialogue 4: Family and Languages (Informal) ​

Dutch:

A: Heb je familie?
B: Ja, ik heb een moeder, een vader en een zus.
A: Is je zus Nederlands?
B: Nee, zij is Turks. Zij spreekt Turks en Nederlands.

Translation:

A: Do you have family?
B: Yes, I have a mother, a father, and a sister.
A: Is your sister Dutch?
B: No, she is Turkish. She speaks Turkish and Dutch.

Reading ​

Read this short text about an introduction. It uses only grammar and vocabulary you've learned in A0-01 and A0-02.

Dutch Text:

Hallo! Ik ben Anna. Ik ben twintig. Ik kom uit Nederland. Ik ben Nederlands. Ik spreek Nederlands en Engels.

Dit is mijn moeder. Zij heet Sophie. Zij is vijfenveertig. Zij komt uit België. Zij is Belgisch. Zij spreekt Nederlands, Frans en Engels.

Dit is mijn vader. Hij heet Jan. Hij is achtenveertig. Hij komt uit Polen. Hij is Pools. Hij spreekt Pools en Nederlands.

Mijn broer is Daan. Hij is achttien. Mijn zus is Emma. Zij is zestien.

Wij zijn een familie. Wij spreken veel talen. Wij zijn gelukkig.

English Translation:

Hello! I am Anna. I am twenty. I am from the Netherlands. I am Dutch. I speak Dutch and English.

This is my mother. She is called Sophie. She is forty-five. She is from Belgium. She is Belgian. She speaks Dutch, French, and English.

This is my father. He is called Jan. He is forty-eight. He is from Poland. He is Polish. He speaks Polish and Dutch.

My brother is Daan. He is eighteen. My sister is Emma. She is sixteen.

We are a family. We speak many languages. We are happy.

Speaking ​

Practice introducing yourself in both informal and formal situations.

Exercise 1: Informal Introduction ​

Scenario: You meet a classmate for the first time.

What you say:

  1. "Hallo. Ik ben [your name]."
  2. "Ik ben [your age]."
  3. "Ik kom uit [your country]."
  4. "Ik spreek [language(s)]."

Model Response:

"Hallo. Ik ben Emma. Ik ben negentien. Ik kom uit Amerika. Ik spreek Engels en een beetje Nederlands."

Exercise 2: Informal Conversation ​

Scenario: A new classmate asks you questions.

They ask: Hoe heet jij?
You respond: Ik ben [your name].

They ask: Ben jij Nederlands?
You respond: Nee, ik ben [your nationality]. (Or: Ja, ik ben Nederlands.)

They ask: Waar kom je vandaan?
You respond: Ik kom uit [your country].

They ask: Heb je familie?
You respond: Ja, ik heb [een moeder, een vader, broers, zussen, etc.].

They ask: Spreek je Engels?
You respond: Ja, ik spreek Engels. Ik spreek ook [other language].

Exercise 3: Formal Introduction ​

Scenario: You meet a teacher or someone older.

What you say:

  1. "Goedemorgen / Goedemiddag."
  2. "Mijn naam is [your name]."
  3. "Ik kom uit [your country]. Ik ben [your nationality]."
  4. "Aangenaam."

Model Response:

"Goedemorgen. Mijn naam is Sophie. Ik kom uit Polen. Ik ben Pools. Aangenaam."

Exercise 4: Partner Interview ​

Work with a partner:

Ask your partner at least 5 of these questions in Dutch. Write down their answers.

  1. Hoe heet jij?
  2. Waar kom je vandaan?
  3. Wat is je nationaliteit?
  4. Hoeveel jaar ben jij?
  5. Heb je familie?
  6. Hoeveel broers en zussen heb je?
  7. Spreek je Engels?
  8. Spreek je andere talen?

Writing ​

Exercise 1: Fill in the Blanks (Present Tense of "Zijn" and "Hebben") ​

Complete each sentence with the correct form of "zijn" or "hebben."

  1. Ik ___ twintig. → ben
  2. U ___ Nederlands. → bent
  3. Hij ___ een broer. → heeft
  4. Wij ___ uit Nederland. → zijn
  5. Zij (she) ___ een zus. → heeft
  6. Jullie ___ Polen. → zijn
  7. Jij ___ een moeder? → heb / hebt
  8. Zij (they) ___ Turks. → zijn
  9. Ik ___ twee broers. → heb
  10. U ___ getrouwd? → bent

Answers: 1. ben 2. bent 3. heeft 4. zijn 5. heeft 6. zijn 7. hebt 8. zijn 9. heb 10. bent

Exercise 2: Convert Statements to Questions ​

Rewrite each statement as a yes/no question using inversion.

  1. Jij bent Emma. → Ben jij Emma?
  2. U bent meneer Jansen. → Bent u meneer Jansen?
  3. Hij is Nederlands. → Is hij Nederlands?
  4. Zij hebben familie. → Hebben zij familie?
  5. Wij zijn uit Frankrijk. → Zijn wij uit Frankrijk?
  6. Jij spreek Engels. → Spreek jij Engels?
  7. U bent getrouwd. → Bent u getrouwd?
  8. Zij is Pools. → Is zij Pools?

Exercise 3: Self-Introduction Paragraph ​

Write a paragraph introducing yourself. Include:

  • Your name
  • Your age
  • Your country of origin
  • Your nationality
  • Language(s) you speak
  • One family fact (mother, father, brother, sister, or whether you're married)

Requirement: Write 5-7 sentences in Dutch. Use at least three forms of "zijn" and two forms of "hebben."

Model Answer:

Hallo! Ik ben Anna. Ik ben twintig. Ik kom uit Nederland. Ik ben Nederlands. Ik spreek Nederlands en Engels. Ik heb een broer. Zijn naam is Daan. Ik ben gelukkig.

Common Mistakes ​

Mistake 1: Confusing "Zijn" and "Hebben" Forms ​

Wrong: Ik is twintig. / Ik hebben een broer.
Right: Ik ben twintig. / Ik heb een broer.
Why: Each pronoun has a specific form. "Ik" always goes with "ben" (not "is") and "heb" (not "hebben").

Wrong: Jij zijn Nederlands. / Jij hebt Nederlands.
Right: Jij bent Nederlands. / Jij spreek Nederlands.
Why: "Jij" goes with "bent" and "hebt." Languages are spoken, not had.

Mistake 2: Mixing Up "Zijn" with English "Have" ​

Wrong: Ik heb twintig jaren. (I have twenty years.)
Right: Ik ben twintig. (I am twenty.)
Why: Dutch uses "zijn" (to be) for age, not "hebben" (to have). English says "I am 20 years old"; Dutch says "Ik ben twintig."

Mistake 3: Not Inverting in Questions ​

Wrong: Jij bent Emma? (with falling intonation, sounds like a statement)
Right: Ben jij Emma? (with rising intonation, sounds like a question)
Why: Dutch requires the verb to come first in yes/no questions. "Jij bent Emma?" can technically be understood as a question by intonation, but the standard form is "Ben jij Emma?"

Mistake 4: Using Wrong Pronoun Formality ​

Wrong: Hoe heet jij? (to your boss or a stranger)
Right: Hoe heet u? (to your boss or a stranger)
Why: "Jij" is for informal situations (friends, classmates, people your age). "U" is for formal situations (strangers, people older than you, people in authority). When in doubt, use "u."

Mistake 5: Forgetting Possessive Pronouns ​

Wrong: Ik naam is Anna. / De naam is Anna.
Right: Mijn naam is Anna.
Why: English can sometimes drop the possessive ("Your name is...?"), but Dutch requires it. "Mijn" is mandatory.

Wrong: Jouw broer is Nederlands. (Sounds awkward)
Right: Je broer is Nederlands. (More natural)
Why: "Je" (unstressed) is more common than "jouw" in everyday speech, though both are correct.

Mistake 6: Wrong Position of "Niet" ​

Wrong: Ik nicht ben Nederlands.
Right: Ik ben niet Nederlands.
Why: "Niet" must come after the main verb or adjective, never before it.

Wrong: Ik ben Nederlands nicht.
Right: Ik ben nicht Nederlands.
Why: "Niet" comes after "ben" (the verb), not after the adjective.

Mistake 7: Confusing "Zij" (She) and "Zij" (They) ​

Wrong: Zij is kinderen. (She is children?)
Right: Zij zijn kinderen. (They are children.)
Why: Context matters. If "zij" refers to multiple people, use "zijn" (plural form). If it refers to one woman, use "is" (singular form).

English clue: If you would say "they are," use "zij zijn" in Dutch. If you would say "she is," use "zij is" in Dutch.

Dutch Insight ​

Formality in Dutch Culture ​

Dutch people are famously direct and informal. In many Dutch companies, classrooms, and social settings, even strangers use "jij" with each other. This doesn't mean formality doesn't exist in Dutch--it does, and "u" is still used in some contexts (older people, formal ceremonies, first meetings with customers, etc.). But Dutch culture values directness and equality, so "jij" is becoming more common overall.

For learners: Use "u" initially. If someone is uncomfortable or if you're in a formal setting, you're safe. If the other person uses "jij" with you or suggests "We can use jij," switch to "jij." You won't offend anyone by being too formal; you might offend them by being too casual.

Languages and Multilingualism ​

The Netherlands is highly multilingual. Most Dutch people under 40 speak English fluently. This is great for visitors but challenging for Dutch learners: people will often switch to English if they hear your accent, which reduces your practice opportunities.

Many Dutch people are proud of their multilingualism and will be impressed if you make an effort to speak Dutch, even if you're not fluent. Phrases like "Ik spreek een beetje Nederlands" (I speak a little Dutch) are common and positive.

Geographic Context for This Lesson's Countries ​

  • Belgium and Germany: Direct neighbors; many Dutch people live or work there. Bilingual (Belgian Dutch and French; German and Danish spoken in Germany).
  • France, Spain, England: Popular travel, study, and business destinations.
  • USA: Major cultural and economic presence in the Netherlands; many Dutch people have family or business ties there.
  • Poland, Romania, Turkey: Large immigrant communities in the Netherlands; you'll likely meet people from these countries if you live in Dutch cities.

This context helps explain why these specific countries and languages appear in introductions: they're practical and relevant to Dutch social reality.

Memory Tricks ​

Trick 1: "Zijn" Conjugation Pattern ​

The verb "zijn" has very irregular forms, but here's a pattern to help remember:

  • ik ben -- Think "I BE"
  • jij bent -- Rhymes with "bent" (as in English "bent")
  • hij/zij/het is -- Think "it IS"
  • wij zijn -- Rhymes with "wine" or "line"

Say them aloud: "ik BEN, jij BENT, hij IS, wij ZIJN." The rhythm helps you remember.

Trick 2: "Hebben" Ends in a Hard Sound ​

All "hebben" forms include the "h" and hard consonant:

  • ik heb -- Ends in "b"
  • jij hebt -- Ends in "t"
  • hij/zij/het heeft -- Ends in "t"
  • wij hebben -- Ends in "n"

Practice saying them fast: "heb, hebt, heeft, hebben." The hard ending consonant is consistent.

Trick 3: "Jij" vs "U" ​

JIJ = INFORMAL (sounds like "yay")
U = FORMAL (sounds like "oo", like "who")

When you use "jij," you're saying "yay!" (excited, informal). When you use "u," your mouth is rounded like "oo" (formal, respectful). This silly trick helps you remember which is which.

Trick 4: Question Word Order ​

STATEMENT: Pronoun + Verb + Rest
"Jij bent Emma."

QUESTION: Verb + Pronoun + Rest
"Ben jij Emma?"

Trick: The verb jumps to the front. Think "Verb First" when you see a question mark.

Trick 5: "Niet" at the End ​

STATEMENT: "Ik ben Nederlands."
NEGATION: "Ik ben NIET Nederlands."

"Niet" comes right after the verb (or adjective). It's like adding a "NOT" stamp after the main word.

Trick 6: "Mijn," "Jouw," "Zijn," "Haar" ​

These are possessives, not pronouns. Think of them as "MY," "YOUR," "HIS," "HER":

  • Mijn naam = My name (mijn sounds like "mine")
  • Jouw naam = Your name (Jouw sounds like "your")
  • Zijn vader = His father (Zijn sounds like "sign")
  • Haar moeder = Her mother (Haar sounds like "hair")

Active Recall ​

Do NOT look at the answers yet. Write or say your responses.

  1. What are the three forms of the verb "zijn" that you need to know?
    (Hint: Think about ik, hij/zij, and wij.)

  2. When do you use "u" instead of "jij"? Give two examples.

  3. What does "Waar kom je vandaan?" mean, and how would you answer it?

  4. How do you ask "Do you have a brother?" in Dutch?

  5. If someone says "Ik ben niet Nederlands," what does that mean?

  6. Rearrange these words into a correct question: "Emma / Ben / jij / ?"

  7. What are the four things you should include in a basic self-introduction in Dutch?

  8. How is the position of "niet" different from English "not"?

Answers:

  1. Three key forms of "zijn": ik ben, hij/zij/het is, wij zijn (There are technically seven forms, but these three cover most conversations.)

  2. Use "u" when: Speaking to someone older than you, a stranger, someone in authority, a customer (if you work in service), or in formal situations. Example: "Hoe heet u?" to a teacher. Example: "Bent u meneer Jansen?" to someone you don't know.

  3. **"Waar kom je vandaan?" means "Where are you from?" You would answer: "Ik kom uit [country]." Example: "Ik kom uit Amerika."

  4. "Do you have a brother?" = "Heb je een broer?" (Heb je = Do you have. Een broer = a brother.)

  5. "Ik ben niet Nederlands" means "I am not Dutch." This is a negation using "zijn."

  6. Correct question: "Ben jij Emma?" (Verb + subject + rest. Not: "Jij ben Emma?")

  7. Four things in a self-introduction:

    • Your name (Ik ben...)
    • Where you're from (Ik kom uit...)
    • Your nationality (Ik ben...)
    • Language(s) you speak (Ik spreek...)

  8. Position of "niet": In English, "not" comes before the verb ("I am NOT Dutch"). In Dutch, "niet" comes after the main verb or complement ("Ik ben NIET Nederlands.").

Quiz ​

Read each question. Write or say your answer. Then check the Answer Key below.

Question 1: Which form of "zijn" matches "ik"? ​

A) is
B) ben
C) zijn
D) bent

Correct Answer: B) ben

Question 2: You want to ask a stranger their name formally. What do you ask? ​

A) Hoe heet jij?
B) Hoe heet u?
C) Wat is jouw naam?
D) Wie ben jij?

Correct Answer: B) Hoe heet u? (The formal "u" instead of informal "jij")

Question 3: How do you form a yes/no question in Dutch? ​

A) Add "do" or "does" like in English
B) Put the verb first, then the subject
C) Change the subject to the end
D) Add a question word at the beginning

Correct Answer: B) Put the verb first, then the subject (e.g., Ben jij Emma?)

Question 4: Which word means "not"? ​

A) nee
B) niet
C) nein
D) ni

Correct Answer: B) niet ("Nee" means "no"; "niet" means "not".)

Question 5: If someone is from Spain, what nationality are they? ​

A) Spaans
B) Spanje
C) Spanjaard
D) Spanjol

Correct Answer: A) Spaans ("Spanje" is the country. "Spaans" is the nationality/language.)

Question 6: Which sentence is correct? ​

A) Ik ben twintig jaren.
B) Ik heb twintig.
C) Ik ben twintig.
D) Ik heb twintig jaren.

Correct Answer: C) Ik ben twintig. (Dutch uses "zijn" for age, not "hebben" like English "have.")

Question 7: How do you say "I have a sister" in Dutch? ​

A) Ik ben een zus.
B) Ik heb een zus.
C) Ik hebben een zus.
D) Ik heb een sister.

Correct Answer: B) Ik heb een zus. (Use "hebben" for possession.)

Question 8: What's the informal pronoun for "you"? ​

A) u
B) jij
C) hij
D) zij

Correct Answer: B) jij ("U" is formal.)

Question 9: Where would "niet" go in this sentence? "Ik ben Nederlands." ​

A) Ik NIET ben Nederlands.
B) Ik ben NIET Nederlands.
C) NIET ik ben Nederlands.
D) Ik ben Nederlands NIET.

Correct Answer: B) Ik ben NIET Nederlands. ("Niet" comes after the verb or adjective.)

Question 10: What does "Waar kom je vandaan?" mean? ​

A) How are you?
B) What's your name?
C) Where are you from?
D) Do you speak Dutch?

Correct Answer: C) Where are you from?

Question 11: If you want to say "I am not German," what do you say? ​

A) Ich bin nicht Deutsch. (wrong language!)
B) Ik ben nicht Duits.
C) Ik ben niet Duits.
D) Ik niet ben Duits.

Correct Answer: C) Ik ben niet Duits. (Note: "niet," not "nicht." And "niet" comes after "ben.")

Question 12: Which pronoun form is used for both "she" AND "they"? ​

A) hij
B) zij
C) wij
D) het

Correct Answer: B) zij (Context tells you if it's "she" or "they.")

Question 13: How do you ask "Do you have a brother?" to a classmate? ​

A) Heb u een broer?
B) Heb je een broer?
C) Hebt je een broer?
D) Have jij een broer?

Correct Answer: B) Heb je een broer? (Informal "je"; "heb" is the right form.)

Question 14: What does "Aangenaam" mean? ​

A) Goodbye
B) Thank you
C) Nice to meet you
D) Excuse me

Correct Answer: C) Nice to meet you

Question 15: Which is a correct self-introduction? ​

A) Hallo. Ik ben Emma. Ik ben achttien. Ik kom uit Amerika. Ik spreek Engels.
B) Hallo. Ik heb Emma. Ik ben achttien. Ik kom uit Amerika. Ik spreek Engels.
C) Hi. I am Emma. I am eighteen. I come from America. I speak English.
D) Hoi. Ik ben Emma. Ik heb achttien. Ik ben van Amerika. Ik kan Engels spreken.

Correct Answer: A) (Uses "zijn" correctly for name and age, "komen uit" for origin, present tense "spreek.")

Homework ​

Do this after completing the lesson. Plan for 30--40 minutes.

Task 1: Memorize the Conjugations ​

Write out the present tense of "zijn" and "hebben" from memory (no peeking at the Grammar section). Then check your work.

Your goal: You should be able to conjugate both verbs without thinking.

Task 2: Personal Introduction in Writing ​

Write a paragraph (6--8 sentences) introducing yourself. Include:

  • Your name
  • Your age
  • Your country of origin
  • Your nationality
  • Two languages you speak (or would like to speak)
  • One family member and their nationality

Requirement: Use at least three different forms of "zijn" and three different forms of "hebben."

Example:

Hallo! Ik ben Anna. Ik ben twintig. Ik kom uit Nederland. Ik ben Nederlands. Ik spreek Nederlands en Engels. Mijn moeder is Belgisch. Zij spreekt Frans. Ik heb een broer. Hij heet Daan. Wij zijn gelukkig.

Task 3: Dialogue Practice ​

Choose one of the four dialogues from the Dialogue section. Practice reading it aloud, paying attention to stress and rhythm. If possible, record yourself and listen.

Your goal: You should be able to read the entire dialogue naturally, without stopping to think about pronunciation.

Task 4: Question and Answer ​

Write 5 yes/no questions you would ask someone when meeting them for the first time. Then write possible answers to each question.

Example Question: Ben jij Nederlands?
Example Answer: Nee, ik ben Pools.

Task 5: Listening Review ​

Listen to the two Listening comprehension dialogues again. Try to understand without reading the transcript first. Then answer the comprehension questions without looking at the answers.

Your goal: You should recognize key words like names, countries, and yes/no responses.

Task 6: Optional Challenge ​

If you're ready for a challenge, find a language exchange partner online and have a 2-3 minute conversation in Dutch where you introduce yourself using what you learned in this lesson. Record it or write down what you said.

Summary ​

Congratulations! You've completed A0-02: Introducing Yourself.

Key Takeaways ​

You now know:

  • ✓ The present tense of "zijn" (to be) and "hebben" (to have)
  • ✓ How to form yes/no questions by putting the verb first
  • ✓ How to introduce yourself: name, age, nationality, origin, languages, family
  • ✓ How to ask others these same questions back
  • ✓ When to use formal "u" vs informal "jij"
  • ✓ How and where to use "niet" for negation
  • ✓ 32 new vocabulary words (names, countries, nationalities, languages, family, numbers 0-20)

What You Can Do Now ​

After this lesson, you can:

  • Introduce yourself in Dutch in a genuine conversation lasting 1--2 minutes
  • Ask and answer basic questions about name, age, nationality, origin, languages, family
  • Understand introductions from other people, even if you don't know every word
  • Correct information about yourself using "nicht" for negation
  • Navigate formal vs. informal situations using "u" or "jij" appropriately

What Comes Next ​

The next lesson is A0-03: Everyday Objects and the "De/Het" Article System. You'll learn:

  • The grammatical gender system in Dutch (why some nouns take "de" and others take "het")
  • Everyday household objects and their articles
  • Plurals and how they change
  • How to describe objects and possessions

In that lesson, you'll take everything you know about pronouns, "zijn," and "hebben" and apply it to describing things: "Dit is een tafel. De tafel is groot. Het huis is klein."

Study Tips for Retention ​

  1. Reread the Dialogue section 3 times. Familiar dialogues make new grammar memorable.
  2. Say the conjugations aloud (zijn and hebben) every morning for a week. Speaking them helps them stick.
  3. Practice introducing yourself to an imaginary person every day.
  4. Write one new sentence in Dutch each day using "zijn," "hebben," or a yes/no question.
  5. Watch Dutch videos or listen to Dutch music. Even if you don't understand most of it, your ear will get used to the rhythm and stress patterns.
